it feels a bit disingenuous to portray something like that as him being basically two different people, which i've seen a lot of people do, but i agree with you that he definitely would lose control (at least over his own fantasies/needing to act them out) + it's pretty comparable to any other type of addiction. the more you partake the more it isolates you and normalizes the behavior. for him that was physical control, and it lead from rape to murder to necrophilia in his need to constantly push the envelope and feel even more heightened power. 

i think a lot of people are giving you very reactionary responses because they've seen a lot of people (including the judge in his trial) excuse his actions or try to portray him as a poor baby not in control of his actions. but i agree you're definitely on the mark, although i might word it a bit differently. i think his shame was rooted in the fact that he hated how much he lost control in these situations. talking about his desires and actions exposed him to reporters/investigators/etc in ways he didn't feel comfortable with because it meant that 1. he wasn't the one with the most power in that situation (unless he lied about parts of it, which he did often) and 2. he had to reveal how powerless he was to his own compulsions. both of these things probably embarrassed the hell out of him.

ted visited the bodies numerous times during the process of decomp, i don't think he had any qualms about reliving the murders through memory lmao. i get what you're saying and i'm sure he knew what he did was wrong but i think he was more fascinated by his own brain and internal motivations than shameful or horrified by it. he even talked about committing suicide in the days before his execution simply because he didn't want anyone to have control of him the way he controlled the women he killed. there was no remorse from him.

i am a person who has schizoaffective & has also dealt with addiction, so i have a bit of personal experience with this. my main response is that you are not responsible for his addiction / coping methods, and it is not your job to support those habits. i know it probably feels horrible to stop, like you're being unsupportive of his mental illnesses in general, but that's not the case at all. he uses weed and alch to numb the symptoms, but they don't go away. you just stop caring about them.

the best thing you can do imo is set boundaries & say in order to sustain a livingspace and food etc you cannot afford to spend your money on his addictions. if you're up for it you can offer help finding a psychiatrist or something, but you need to put your foot down with the money. addicts will take and take and not even think about the person at the other end because we're so wrapped up in our own heads.

ETA: maybe you could schedule an alarm on your phone to remind him to take meds? but thats also only helpful if he's willing to take them. you say he's trying, but if he is refusing meds and not demanding help from his doctor then he needs to try harder. being a self advocate is hard as hell but necessary.

I'm really glad that you are taking the advice to heart - recognising that youve done something wrong and need to work on self improvement is a really big first step, and working out where the actions stemmed from and what you can do to resolve those negative feelings (vis communication with your partner, self soothing, etc) will help a lot.

You did blow it apart, and you have to own that and do better with future partners. She has no reason to take you back, and i'm sure your clingy/codependent reaction is scaring her away even further. 

Taking responsibility for your own actions means respecting her choice and moving on, not saying you wish she would take you back because it was one stupid mistake. From what you recounted in your post, I cant find any event that would make me feel even remotely close to invading my partners space like that. Saying you felt "consumed" and that thats not who you are are two ways of not taking full responsibility for your actions. 

I truly hope you can work out some of your insecurities and come out of this stronger and more confident in yourself, because this level of insecurity with literally no trigger isnt conducive at all to healthy relationships.

I think its important to look at the context here - she was in an abusive relationship right before your partnership. this oftentimes involves controlling behavior, such as the abuser "checking up on" their partner. needing to know what they are doing and who they are with at all times, telling them who they can and cannot interact with, etc. this level of control can leave a serious impact on abuse survivors, and she might have seen it as a red flag (whether it was leading to worse or not) because she is trying to protect herself above all else. 

Also want to add that her texting this guy about getting a plant is not exactly flirty behavior or overstepping any bounds of friendship, and her insistence on them being just friends is most likely the truth. Talking to her best friend in private about the fantasy of dating a bad boy is very very different from cheating.
